title: Endpoint Day-Zero Ops Decision Frames
content:
Purpose:
Quick, tactical note for field and product on how to frame Day-Zero operational decisions when customers compare hyperscaler managed endpoints (AWS/GCP/Azure) vs Redwood. This is intentionally conversational — use as a cheat-sheet in calls and pitch prep.

Audience:
- Sales engineering (SE) and field AEs prepping discovery and technical scoping
- Product marketing for 1-pagers and internal enablement
- Solutions and onboarding teams for proposal scoping

Thesis (one-liner):
Customers choose hyperscaler endpoints for convenience and consolidation; they choose Redwood for predictable production inference economics, deterministic SLAs, and escape hobbled operational ownership (no surprise throttles, opaque cost spikes, or poor KV/memory controls).

Day-zero decision frames (how customers think):
1) "I need it now, on the cloud I already trust"
   - H: single-console, marketplace listing, one-click host
   - Risk: opaque per-token cost behavior across scaling, limited escape routes if latency or quality regressions occur
   - Redwood hook: get them to quantify peak vs tail latency tolerance and token economics. If tail latency or predictable throughput matters, offer a Dedicated baseline to remove burst uncertainty.

2) "We need isolation + compliance"
   - H: VPC + marketplace offerings often marketed as private but still share control planes or telemetry with provider
   - Risk: hidden dependency on hyperscaler-managed control plane for upgrades/backups; limited KMS/HSM flexibility
   - Redwood hook: emphasize private deployment blueprint (control plane options, on-prem packaging, flexible KMS integrations) and audit log fidelity.

3) "Cost will be the first knife fight"
   - H: hyperscalers will pitch consolidation and discounts; they bury unit economics in model selection + GPU flavor + burst policy
   - Risk: unpredictable autoscaling + opaque batching defaults drive cost above committed expectation
   - Redwood hook: show token-unit economics, batching/caching levers, and a modeled scenario (QPS/seq-len mix) that demonstrates 20–40% unit cost delta at production scale.

4) "Reliability under load or model rollout"
   - H: managed endpoints can surface as SLA but often have coarse-grained fallbacks and long rollback paths
   - Risk: slow canary changes, limited model-variant routing controls, poor observability at per-route level
   - Redwood hook: rollout primitives (canary/A-B, automatic fallback to cheaper compatible variant), tracing hooks with token-level cost/latency and per-route dashboards.

Practical win themes to deploy in pitch (short bullets):
- Predictable unit economics: we give a modeled bill for real workload shapes (not list price)
- Deterministic latency SLOs +/- regional fallback: you decide the tradeoff, not the provider
- Operational ownership: tooling to diagnose KV cache pressure, per-route batching, and eviction strategies
- Private-first architecture: control plane and KMS flexibility for regulated workloads
- Smooth escape hatch: can run same config in hosted, dedicated, private with minimal rewrite

Objection handling (quick scripts):
- "Hyperscaler discounts will beat you": ask for a 3-month workload trace; show steady-state vs tail cost and where batching/caching moves the needle. Avoid sticker-price debate.
- "We want one vendor to rule infra": acknowledge the desire but highlight single-point-of-failure risk and SLA surface area; for regulated or high-traffic apps, show joint-mode (Redwood Dedicated in their VPC) as a compromise.
- "We already have ML infra": pivot to operational gaps (runtime ops, rollout controls, quality regressions) and propose a 6-week pilot with synthetic load + real prompts.

Signals to probe in discovery (questions to ask customers):
- Peak QPS and 95/99/99.9 latency expectations for key routes
- Sequence length distribution and how often long-tail generations occur
- Model change velocity (how often do you swap model weights or tune prompts?)
- Audit/compliance requirements: retention windows, KMS/HSM needs, on-prem constraints
- Cost budgeting approach: committed monthly budget vs elastic spend vs unit-event accounting

Battle cards (what to share internally before a demo):
- Benchmark snippet: our 1000 QPS, 8–16 seq len mix cost model (attach in appendix / benchmarks PR)
- Typical migration plan: seed pilot -> dedicated/commitment sizing -> private rollout timeline
- Escalation matrix: when to call product engineering vs solutions eng vs SRE for capacity or kernel issues

Short checklist for SE before call:
- Ask for a small trace or sample prompts (real prompt shapes beat synthetic)
- Prep a conservative cost model that includes tail autoscale buffer
- Load the right model in demo: show Redwood trace/latency dashboard and fallback behavior live

Competitive differentiators (practical wording for slides):
- Not just "managed" — controllable managedness: precise knobs for batching, cache TTLs, and model routing
- Open-model friendly: curated model catalog but with transparent performance profiles and upgrade windows
- Production playbooks: baseline templates for SLOs, canary rollouts, and cost-regression alerts tied to evaluation prompts

Known gaps to be honest about (so field has a consistent message):
- Global reach: hyperscalers have broader global infra – call that out and offer partner/cloud-region plans for most geos
- Some customers prefer consolidated billing; provide guidance for hybrid cost reporting
- Extremely tiny projects (<$500/mo): hosted hyperscaler convenience can be a faster low-friction choice

Open questions & next steps (internal):
- Create a small sample cost workbook for 3 workload archetypes (chat-heavy, embedding-heavy, batch-transform)
- Generate a one-page pilot SOW template for Dedicated pilots with default commit tiers and rollback clauses
- Coordinate with benchmarks PR to add a 95/99 latency cost projection table we can share in sales decks (assign Rohit)

Appendix / quick notes to self:
- Keep canned examples short: 1 chat route (QPS 50, median len 40 tokens), 1 embed route (throughput 2000 vectors/hr), 1 batch (hourly batch of 10k).
- Store a sanitized trace template in Confluence linked_artifacts above.

Bottom line (elevator):
If a customer cares about "predictable production inference" — not just model access — lead with operational levers (batching, KV cache control, quantization guidance) + deterministic economics. Hyperscalers win on friction; Redwood wins on long-term cost certainty and playbooked reliability.

Notes-to-self: polish into 1-pager + cheat-cards for SEs before end of Q1.
